The other day, I found an old journal tucked beneath a pile of books in my attic. The pages were yellowed with time, the ink faded like a half-remembered dream. I flipped through it, half-expecting to see my own handwriting—but no, this was someone else’s. The first entry was dated 1987, and it began with a single sentence: *"Today, I learned that the world is not as it seems."*

I don’t know who wrote it, but the words pulled me in. The journal was a patchwork of observations—some profound, some mundane. There were sketches of constellations with names I didn’t recognize, scribbled notes about "the hum beneath the silence," and a recurring theme of doors that led nowhere. The last entry was just a question: *"What happens when we stop looking for answers?"*

It made me think about how often we chase explanations, as if the universe owes us clarity. We label things—good, bad, love, loss—like they’re fixed, when really, they’re just moments suspended in time. The journal’s owner seemed to understand that. They wrote about the way light bends through a glass of water, how a single raindrop can hold an entire sky, and how sometimes the most ordinary things—like the scent of rain on pavement—carry the weight of something infinite.

I closed the journal and set it back on the shelf, wondering if I’d ever find another like it. Maybe the point isn’t to seek meaning but to let it find us, like a leaf drifting to the ground. Or maybe the real mystery isn’t out there at all, but in the quiet spaces between our thoughts, where the world hums just a little louder than we realize.
